title: The physician from the unseen
hookLine: a holy physician takes her pulse while naming cities, and at Samarkand it leaps (Masnavi 1)
tomorrow: a hard ending, read as allegory

lines: THE GOOD ONES LISTEN TO YOUR LIFE.
A DREAM ON THE PRAYER MAT.
cards: Some doctors listen to your chest. The good ones also listen to your life. You go in for headaches, and the right question isn't which pills you're taking.

It's how's work, how are you sleeping, is anything going on at home? Back to the king, weeping on the prayer mat. He falls asleep there, and in a dream an old man tells him: tomorrow a stranger will come.
He is a true physician. Trust him. Today, the physician from the unseen.

teach.b: Next morning the stranger appears. The king doesn't wait on his throne; he goes out himself and embraces him like an old friend.
The physician sits by the girl, looks at her color, takes her pulse, and understands at once: the other doctors didn't make her worse by accident.

teach.h: THE ILLNESS IS IN THE HEART.
teach.b: They were treating the body, and the illness is in the heart. So he asks the king to clear the house. No family, no servants, just the two of them.
He talks to her gently, the way you'd talk to someone from out of town. Where are you from? Who were your friends there?
All the while, his fingers stay on her pulse. He names towns, one after another, and the pulse stays still.
Then he says Samarkand, and her pulse leaps, and her face goes red, then pale.

A few more gentle questions and he knows: she loves a goldsmith in Samarkand, and she's been homesick and heartsick since the day she was brought away. He tells her not to worry, and to keep it secret.

There's an echo here. Persian literature had an older story of the great physician Ibn Sina, called Avicenna in the West, who found a young man's hidden love the same way, by his pulse, naming streets and houses.
Rumi may be drawing on a tale his listeners knew.

teach.h: THE GUIDE LISTENS FOR THE SECRET.
teach.b: Sufi readers see more: the physician from the unseen is the true spiritual guide, who knows that what hurts us is often what we secretly love, and listens for it. The secret was near the lament, remember?
You find it where the pulse leaps.

how: Sufi teachers read the divine physician as the figure of the true spiritual guide, and the pulse scene is among the best-known episodes of the Masnavi's opening story.

o: the great physician Ibn Sina, by his Western name
the goldsmith the girl loves in Samarkand
the old man who speaks in the king's dream

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: the old man in the dream
clears the house, takes her pulse

s: the physician finds her illness is in the heart
the others treated the body; the illness was love and longing.
he names her illness in front of the whole court
he asks the king to clear the house, and talks with her alone.
Sufi readers see only a medical story here
they see the true spiritual guide, who listens for what the soul secretly loves.

games.q: you're the physician. the girl is too frightened to say what's wrong. what do you do?
o: talk gently about her hometowns, fingers on her pulse.
games.why: he asks about towns and friends, one by one, holding her pulse. at Samarkand it leaps, and he knows.

practice: Pick something that's been bothering you, tiredness, a short temper, a knot in the stomach, and rest your attention on your body as if your fingers were on your own pulse.
Gently name possible causes one at a time: work, money, a person, a place you miss, something you want and haven't said. Notice which name makes something leap, and don't fix it yet; just know it.

wordCard.voice: Avicenna. The physician Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, whose older tale of finding hidden love by the pulse echoes here. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, from Arabic: physician. in the Sufi reading, the true guide of the soul.

carryVoice: Your line: where the pulse leaps. The good physician listens for it. That's day one hundred seventy-two.
